title: Jeremiah 52:1–11
context: After the note that closes chapter 51, “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah,” the narrator tells how Zedekiah reigned eleven years, did evil as Jehoiakim had, and rebelled against Babylon, how Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem until famine came and the wall was breached, and how Zedekiah fled but was overtaken in the plains of Jericho and brought to Riblah. There the king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons and the princes of Judah, blinded Zedekiah, and took him to Babylon, where he was kept in prison until he died. The account closely parallels 2 Kings 24:18–25:7 and Jeremiah 39:1–7, which are named here without harmonizing, and both traditions read it soberly as shared ground: the judgment the LORD announced through his prophets came to pass, and the suffering is told plainly rather than dwelt on.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign. He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign. He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the narrator now speaks, after 51:64 marks the end of Jeremiah’s words.

The same notice appears in 2 Kings 24:18.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the last king of Judah introduced in the familiar pattern, including his mother Hamutal.

Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a historical appendix confirming that Jeremiah’s word about Jerusalem was fulfilled.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah is responsible for his choices.

The book has shown his repeated reluctance to heed Jeremiah (cf. 38:14–23).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the same verdict that marked the reigns before him.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the king’s evil is real and his own, continuing the pattern that led to judgment.

verses.text: For through the LORD’s anger this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For through the LORD’s anger this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence.” Arminian readers note that the narrator places Zedekiah’s rebellion within God’s judgment.

His choice remains real.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s anger governing the events, with Zedekiah’s rebellion as the means.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the judgment had been announced, that Zedekiah is responsible, and that God is just in what follows, as in the parallel notes at 2 Kings 24:20.

verses.text: In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it round about.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came.” Arminian readers note the careful date, also given in 39:1 and 2 Kings 25:1.

The date marks the gravity of the event.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the siege as a turning point in Judah’s history.

Shared ground: both traditions read the siege as the final stage of the judgment the LORD had announced, while the city still had time to heed Jeremiah’s counsel (cf. 38:17).

verses.text: So the city was besieged to the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the city was besieged to the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.” Arminian readers note the length of the siege.

The narrator gives the duration without describing its suffering in detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the long siege as part of the sober account of judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse plainly, letting its brevity stand and avoiding speculation about what the city endured.

verses.text: In the fourth month, in the ninth day of the month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says that in the fourth month “the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.” Arminian readers note the suffering of ordinary people.

The date matches 39:2 and 2 Kings 25:3.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the famine as part of the covenant warnings given long before (cf. Lev 26:26).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion for the people of the land, who bore the hardship of the city’s fall.

verses.text: Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled, and went out of the city by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden. Now the Chaldeans were against the city all around. The men of war went toward the Arabah,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled.” Arminian readers note the collapse of the city’s defense.

The flight “by the way of the gate between the two walls” is also described in 39:4.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the soldiers’ flight as the failure of human strength against the LORD’s word (cf. 38:18).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as narrative, naming the parallels without pressing small differences of detail.

verses.text: but the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says “the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho.” Arminian readers note that the king’s escape fails.

His army is scattered from him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s warning that Zedekiah would not escape (cf. 34:3).

Shared ground: both traditions read the capture plainly as the outcome Jeremiah had warned of, without adding detail.

verses.text: Then they took the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he pronounced judgment on him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then they took the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he pronounced judgment on him.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah faces the king he rebelled against.

Riblah served as the Babylonian command center.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the rebellion of 52:3 meeting its consequence.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, noting that Jeremiah had said Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon face to face (cf. 34:3).

verses.text: The king of Babylon killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. He also killed all the princes of Judah in Riblah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Babylon killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes. He also killed all the princes of Judah in Riblah.” Arminian readers state this plainly and with grief.

The text reports the deaths briefly, and no further detail is added.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse with sobriety and sorrow.

Shared ground: both traditions refuse to dwell on the cruelty, recognize the real loss of these lives, and note the parallels in 39:6 and 2 Kings 25:7.

verses.text: He put out the eyes of Zedekiah; and the king of Babylon bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon, and put him in prison until the day of his death.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He put out the eyes of Zedekiah; and the king of Babylon bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon.” Arminian readers note that Zedekiah is kept in prison “until the day of his death.”

The parallels are 39:7 and 2 Kings 25:7.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly, and some connect it with Ezekiel 12:13, which spoke of the king being brought to Babylon without seeing it.

Shared ground: both traditions state the blinding plainly and without expansion, as the end of Judah’s last king.
